wording: A meta-analysis of prospective cohorts found religiosity/spirituality associated with reduced mortality in initially healthy populations (combined HR 0.82, 0.76–0.87) but not in diseased populations (HR 0.98, 0.94–1.01).
counterevidence_limits: Abstract-only access (T08); Cycle-1 rule caps abstract-only claims at Plausible. Full-text cohort evidence for the association is in C1-R4-01/02.

wording: That religious participation causally lowers mortality remains a hypothesis. counterevidence_limits: Reverse causation (healthier people attend more) and confounding by social integration remain live alternatives.

wording: In pooled data from two US cohorts, weekly religious-service attendance vs never was associated with 26% lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.84), with an E-value of 2.04 for the point estimate, in an outcome-wide design.
counterevidence_limits: Observational; E-value bounds but does not detect confounding.

wording: Among US health professionals, at-least-weekly attendance vs never was associated with lower hazard of deaths from despair (drugs, alcohol, suicide): HR 0.32 (0.16-0.62) in women (NHSII) and 0.67 (0.48-0.94) in men (HPFS); the authors report E-values of 5.70 and 2.35.
counterevidence_limits: Health-professional cohorts; small numbers of events.

wording: Challenge: in a Swedish population cohort (n = 24,855), past-year attendance was associated with lower all-cause mortality until social-participation items were introduced into the model; the authors suggest a social-network pathway in a highly secularized country.
counterevidence_limits: 13.9% attenders; one country; adjustment for mediators can also remove genuine pathway effects.
verification_phrases: V14|until social participation items were introduced in the final model || V14|social network pathway
